tests.name: Quick Check
tests.description: Timed check on Prose Set Texts

questions.question: Q: Name three common prose authors studied at GCSE Latin.
questions.correctAnswer: Caesar (De Bello Gallico), Cicero (speeches and letters), Tacitus (Annales), Pliny the Younger (Letters), Livy (Ab Urbe Condita) (any three).

questions.question: Q: What is the subject of Caesar's De Bello Gallico?
questions.correctAnswer: Caesar's own account of his military campaigns in Gaul (58-50 BC), covering battles, negotiations with Gallic tribes, and expeditions to Britain and Germany.

questions.question: Q: What was the Catilinarian conspiracy and which author wrote about it?
questions.correctAnswer: A plot led by Catiline to overthrow the Roman Republic in 63 BC, exposed by Cicero in his In Catilinam speeches. Cicero's four orations against Catiline are a key set text option.

tests.name: Exam-Style Practice
tests.description: Short-answer practice on Prose Set Texts

questions.question: Q: What does Pliny's letter about Vesuvius describe?
questions.correctAnswer: Pliny the Younger describes the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79, which his uncle Pliny the Elder died investigating. It is a key eyewitness account of the disaster.

questions.question: Q: How often do set texts change?
questions.correctAnswer: Set texts typically change every two years. You must check your exam board's specification for the current prescribed texts for your year of examination.

questions.question: Q: What is the typical length of a prose set text prescription?
questions.correctAnswer: Approximately 110-120 lines of Latin text, as prescribed by the exam board.

questions.question: Q: What themes are common in Tacitus's writing?
questions.correctAnswer: The corruption of imperial power, tyranny vs freedom, the relationship between emperor and Senate, moral decline under the principate, and the loss of Republican libertas.

questions.question: Q: Why is understanding the author's purpose important?
questions.correctAnswer: Because each author writes with a specific agenda: Caesar writes to justify and glorify his own achievements; Cicero writes to persuade and defend; Tacitus writes to critique imperial power. Recognising purpose helps you analyse the text's reliability, bias, and literary construction.
